questions.text:
In a B+ tree, the requirement of at least half-full (50%) node occupancy is relaxed
for which one of the following cases?
questions.solution:
In a B+ tree of order [latex]m[/latex], every node (internal or leaf) must be at least half full [latex]\text{---}[/latex] except the root.

The root can have as few as 2 children (or just 1 key if it is a leaf), otherwise a small tree could never be built.

Answer: Only the root node

questions.text:
Which of the following statements about a relation R in first normal form (1NF)
is/are TRUE ?
questions.solution:
1NF only requires every attribute value to be atomic (no multi-valued or composite attributes).

- R can have a multi-attribute key [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (e.g. key (roll_no, course_id)). This is about keys, not about values.
- R cannot have a foreign key [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE, 1NF puts no restriction on foreign keys.
- R cannot have a composite attribute [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE, a composite attribute is non-atomic and must be split into simple attributes.
- R cannot have more than one candidate key [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: R can have a multi-attribute key; R cannot have a composite attribute

questions.text: Let [latex]L_1, L_2 [/latex] be two regular languages and [latex]L_3 [/latex] a language which is not regular. Which of the following statements is/are always TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- [latex]L_1\cap\overline{L_2}=\phi[/latex] only means [latex]L_1\subseteq L_2[/latex]. Equality also needs [latex]L_2\subseteq L_1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- [latex]L_1\cup L_3[/latex] can be regular: take [latex]L_1=\Sigma^*[/latex], then [latex]L_1\cup L_3=\Sigma^*[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE (not always).
- If [latex]\overline{L_3}[/latex] were regular, then its complement [latex]L_3[/latex] would be regular (closure under complement). So [latex]\overline{L_3}[/latex] is not regular [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Regular languages are closed under complement and union, so [latex]\overline{L_1}\cup\overline{L_2}[/latex] is regular [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: [latex]\overline{L_3}[/latex] is not regular; [latex]\overline{L_1}\cup\overline{L_2}[/latex] is regular

questions.text: Which of the following statements about threads is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Threads can also be implemented in user space (user-level threads) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- The file descriptor table belongs to the process and is shared by all its threads [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Every thread has its own stack (and registers, PC) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Threads share the same address space, so one thread can read/overwrite another thread's data; there is no protection between them [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Threads belonging to a process are by default not protected from each other

questions.text: Which of the following process state transitions is/are NOT possible?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Running [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Ready: possible (preemption / time slice over).
- Waiting [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Running: NOT possible. When the I/O finishes, the process goes to Ready; only the scheduler can move it to Running.
- Ready [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Waiting: NOT possible. A process can block (request I/O) only while it is running.
- Running [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Terminated: possible (exit).

Answer: Waiting to Running, Ready to Waiting
